newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS - Brazil braces for bleak trade numbers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Brazil braces for bleak trade numbers.

text.p: Brazil's surprisingly high $655 million trade deficit in September has further soured the nation's trade outlook, with many economists now saying the trade gap could swell to $4.0 billion by year's end.
"(September's deficit) is big, but it's not the big surprise. October will be even worse," said Dany Rappaport, chief economist for MCM Consultores in Brazil.
Rappaport said Brazil's October trade gap would rise to somewhere between $900 million and $1.0 billion on more consumer good imports for Christmas and other seasonal factors.

The government blamed September's large deficit on unexpectedly high petroleum product imports by state oil monopoly Petrobras. It said Petrobras may have been stockpiling due to fears of a possible strike ahead of wage negotiations this month.
But officials said the one-time surge in oil imports would not affect trade accounts in coming months, which would show healthier balances.
Most economists, however, said trade numbers would get worse before they get better.

"The government may be right that oil imports won't have such a negative effect next month. But there are other factors that are going to take their place," said Mauro Schneider, chief economist for ING Bank in Brazil.
Schneider said that in addition to the Christmas season, imports were generally on the rise due to a steady recovery of the Brazilian economy, which was stagnant throughout most of the first half.

Former Central Bank president and leading Brazilian economist Afonso Celso Pastore said the government's explanation for the worsening trade picture, which pressures the current account, has been inadequate.

"One month it's oil, another month it's sardines. What's it going to be next month, French fries?" Pastore told Jornal do Brasil newspaper. "I'm looking for a more substantive comment from the government, not excuses."

Although the September trade gap was surprising, economists said it was not alarming. They said it was natural for Brazil, which has increasingly opened up its economy over the past five years, to run trade deficits while domestic industry becomes more competitive.

"A $3.0 billion trade deficit for 1996 is bad, $4.0 billion is worse, but there is no magic number which is going to mean the end of the world," said ING's Schneider, who forecasts a year-end deficit of close to $4.0 billion.

But economists warned that Brazil could continue to run up large trade deficits only as long as external conditions remain favorable. If global interest rates began to soar and economic growth in the industrialized nations slowed significantly, Brazil would lose its tolerance for steep deficits, they said.
